## The Open Question

Could some of our language change results, especially those involving centralization (back vowel fronting, the Low Back Merger Shift, American Raising) be biased by the fact younger people talk faster?
[@Kendall2009; @Kendall2013a; @kendallSociophoneticsSpeechRate2023]

## The Upshot

::: incremental
- Yes, both conceptually and empirically (in some case studies), the generational effect appears to be biased in this way.

- We can get less biased generational change estimates if we include average vowel duration by speaker (*not* token duration!) in our models.

- We should start thinking about Causal Inference to avoid potential pitfalls like this.
:::

## Causal Inference

> Correlation does not imply causation.

::: fragment
But...
would you really care to listen to me yammer about quantitative [\*\~\*associations\*\~\*]{.fancy} that you *shouldn't*[^1] interpret causally in any way?
:::

## Causal Inference

By pre-specifying a causal model, we can identify potential confounds, and adjust for them.

::::: {layout-ncol="2"}
::: {}
Backdoor causal path

```{r}

rate |>
```

## Age & Rate Backdoor

```{typst}
#import "def_dag.typ": dag, blue, red, green
#set text(font: "Public Sans")

#dag(
  fills: (
    "dob": blue, "vq": blue,
    "age": red, "dur": red,
    "adur": red, "arate": red
  ),
  strokes: (
    "dob->vq": blue+2pt,
    "age->vq": red+2pt,
    "dob->age": red+2pt,
    "dur->vq": red+2pt,
    "adur->dur": red+2pt,
    "arate->adur": red+2pt,
    "age->arate": red+2pt
  )
)
```

## Age Backdoor

```{r}
sym_limits <- function(x){
  max_l <- x |> abs() |> max()
  c(-max_l, max_l)
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-asp: 1
#| fig-align: center
ests |> 
  filter(
    mod == "~dob"
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(
      estimate
    )
  ) + 
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  stat_slab(
    density = "histogram",
    aes(
      fill = after_stat(-x)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "vp ~ dob"
  ) +
  scale_fill_continuous(
    limits = sym_limits,
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(-2.6, 2.6),
    breaks = c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2),
    labels = c("-2", "-1", "<b style='font-size:16pt;'>0</b>", "1", "2")
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = "none"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~term, label = "label_both")  +
  theme_no_y() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_markdown()
  )
```

## A centralizing change: American Raising in Philadelphia {.smaller}

- Data extracted from the Philadelphia Neighborhood Corpus using new-fave.

- Nearey normalized with `{tidynorm}`.

- Filtered to just white speakers' pre-voiceless /ay/ tokens

```{r}
ay0_dat <- read_csv("data/ay0_dat.csv")
```

```{r}
ay0_dat |> 
  select(
    idstring, gender, dob
  ) |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    gender = replace_values(
      gender,
      "m" ~ "men",
      "f" ~ "women"
    )
  ) |> 
  summarise(
    .by = c(idstring,gender, dob),
    n = n()
  ) |> 
  summarise(
    .by = gender,
    speakers = n(),
    `median tokens/speaker` = median(n),
    `total tokens` = sum(n),
    dob_low = min(dob),
    dob_hi = max(dob)
  ) |> 
  unite(
    dob_low:dob_hi,
    col = "dob range",
    sep = " to "
  ) |> 
  tt() |> 
  format_tt(
    j = "total tokens",
    num_mark_big = ",",
    digit = 2
  )  |> 
  style_tt(
    j = 2:4,
    align = "r"
  )
```

- All models fit with `{brms}` with random intercepts by speaker and word.

- Interactions with gender were included for DOB, and age when it was included.

## A centralizing change: American Raising in Philadelphia

As a centralizing change, the speech rate back door could lead to *overestimating* the DOB effect.

## American Raising Results

```{r}
ay0_noage_mod <- read_rds(here::here("models/ay0_age_mod.rds"))
ay0_nodur_mod <- read_rds(here::here("models/ay0_nodur_mod.rds"))
ay0_ldur_mod <- read_rds(here::here("models/ay0_ldur_mod.rds"))
ay0_full_mod <- read_rds(here::here("models/ay0_flat_mod.rds"))
```

```{r}
list(
  `dob` = ay0_noage_mod,
  `dob, age` = ay0_nodur_mod,
  `dob, age, dur` = ay0_ldur_mod,
  `dob, age, adur` = ay0_full_mod
) |> 
  map(
    ~ .x |> 
      #set_modeldata(ay0_dat |> select(-group)) |> 
      comparisons(
      newdata = datagrid(gender = unique, age = 45),
      variables = list(
        dob = 25
      ),
      by = "gender",
      re_formula = NA
    ) |> 
      get_draws()
  ) |> 
  list_rbind(
    names_to = "mod"
  ) ->
  all_comp
```

```{r}
all_comp |> 
  mutate(
    mod = fct_reorder(mod, -draw),
    gender = replace_values(
      gender,
      "f" ~ "women",
      "m" ~ "men"
    )
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(draw, fill = mod, group = mod)
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    aes(group = "dob")
  ) +
  stat_slab(
    color = "black"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "dob+25 estimate",
    guide = guide_axis(angle = -45, check.overlap = T),
    breaks = c(-0.1, -0.05, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_tight() +  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = adjust_transparency(
        c(ptol_red, ptol_blue, ptol_purple, ptol_green),
        alpha = 0.6
      ),
    limits = rev    
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~gender) +
  theme_no_y() +
  theme_sub_legend(
    position = "top"
  ) +
  theme_sub_panel(
    border = element_rect()
  ) -> p

reveal_groups(
  p, 
  order = c(1, 6,5,4,3,2)
) ->
  plots
```

## American Raising Results

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
preds |>
```

## A peripheralizing change: /ey/ Raising in Philadelphia {.smaller}

- Data extracted from the Philadelphia Neighborhood Corpus using new-fave.

- Nearey normalized with `{tidynorm}`.

- Filtered to just white speakers' pre-consonantal /ey/.

```{r}
ey <- read_csv("data/ey_dat.csv")
```

```{r}
ey |> 
  select(
    idstring, gender, dob
  ) |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    gender = replace_values(
      gender,
      "m" ~ "men",
      "f" ~ "women"
    )
  ) |> 
  summarise(
    .by = c(idstring,gender, dob),
    n = n()
  ) |> 
  summarise(
    .by = gender,
    speakers = n(),
    `median tokens/speaker` = median(n),
    `total tokens` = sum(n),
    dob_low = min(dob),
    dob_hi = max(dob)
  ) |> 
  unite(
    dob_low:dob_hi,
    col = "dob range",
    sep = " to "
  ) |> 
  tt() |> 
  format_tt(
    j = "total tokens",
    num_mark_big = ",",
    digit = 2
  )  |> 
  style_tt(
    j = 2:4,
    align = "r"
  )
```

- All models fit with `{brms}` with random intercepts by speaker and word.

- Interactions with gender were included for DOB, and age when it was included.

## A peripheralizing change: /ey/ Raising in Philadelphia

As a peripheralizing change, the speech rate back door could lead us to *underestimating* the DOB effect.

```{r}
ey_full_mod <- read_rds(here::here("models/ey_all_mod.rds"))
```

```{r}
list(
  `dob` = ey_noage_mod,
  `dob, age, adur` = ey_full_mod
) |> 
  map(
    ~ .x |> 
      #set_modeldata(ay0_dat |> select(-group)) |> 
      comparisons(
      newdata = datagrid(gender = unique, age = 45),
      variables = list(
        dob = 25
      ),
      by = "gender",
      re_formula = NA
    ) |> 
      get_draws()
  ) |> 
  list_rbind(
    names_to = "mod"
  ) ->
  ey_all_comp
```

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-asp: 0.7
#| fig-format: svg
ey_all_comp |> 
  mutate(
    mod = fct_reorder(mod, draw),
    gender = replace_values(
      gender,
      "f" ~ "women",
      "m" ~ "men"
    )
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(draw, fill = mod, group = mod)
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    aes(group = "dob")
  ) +
  stat_slab(
    color = "black"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "dob+25 estimate",
    guide = guide_axis(angle = -45, check.overlap = T),
    breaks = c(-0.1, -0.05, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_tight() +  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = adjust_transparency(
        c(ptol_red, ptol_green),
        alpha = 0.6
      ),
    limits = rev    
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~gender) +
  theme_no_y() +
  theme_sub_legend(
    position = "top"
  ) +
  theme_sub_panel(
    border = element_rect()
  )
```

## Conclusions

- It would be a good idea to include average vowel duration by speaker in our statistical models of language change.

- We should probably start laying out our causal models more explicitly, since not doing so can lead us to both over- and underestimate effects of interest.
